Row.Text: Gilgamesh, king of the Sumerian city-state Uruk, did not exist in the way that we know him today. Yet he remains a profoundly influential figure as the hero of the oldest surviving epic. This story exists in fragments, yet tells a moving tale of arrogance, heroism, loss, and grief that remains deeply relatable over four thousand years since it was first pressed into clay.

The Epic of Gilgamesh, especially its later Akkadian version, relates how the vain king’s cruelty provokes the ire of the gods, who send a wild man, Enkidu, to be Gilgamesh’s bane. But Gilgamesh and Enkidu, after testing their strength against each other, become close friends, and set out across the Sumerian landscape defeating monsters.

Gilgamesh’s strength – and perhaps his luxurious beard – draws the attention of the goddess Ishtar. Gilgamesh does not return her affections, a wise move given the unfortunate fate of Ishtar’s former lovers, and the slighted goddess sends the Bull of Heaven to attack the two friends. But Gilgamesh and Enkidu defeat the bull, and Enkidu adds to the insult by flinging the bull’s leg at the goddess, turning her personal grievance into an offense against the authority of the gods themselves.

The gods respond by sending Enkidu a fatal illness. The two friends lament their fate, cursing all of the people and events that have brought them to this point, and when Enkidu finally succumbs, Gilgamesh’s grief over the death of his friend resonates to this day: he calls his former enemy the axe at his side, the robe on his back, and calls upon all the people and animals of the land to weep. After the wild man’s passing, Gilgamesh becomes terrified of his own mortality and embarks on a fruitless quest to find the elixir of life.

We know the Epic through a series of tablets, dating from the Sumerian period to the Babylonian and later Akkadian periods – it is the Akkadian Gilgamesh presented here. The most significant find was the discovery in 1853 CE of the Epic in the library of the seventh century BCE Assyrian king Ashurbanipal. That Ashurbanipal preserved the Epic is a testament to the staying power of the story: Ashurbanipal’s version was written over a thousand years after the earliest surviving copy.

Was Gilgamesh real? Sumerian king lists do mention a Gilgamesh of Uruk around 2900 BCE, but little other connection exists between the heroic Gilgamesh and any historical figure. Uruk at the time was a city-state in present-day Iraq, and ruled over an increasingly restive land near the end of its height. It would have been a fortress of urban life in a very different world, one with few cities and vast stretches outside of state control – wild men and forest-monsters, indeed. Nonetheless, its voice still calls to us, telling us that humanity’s time on earth is brief, and even the strongest among us fall.
